title: How To Regain Calm When You're Feeling Stressed Out https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2017/09/30/how-to-regain-calm-when-youre-feeling-stressed/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin introduces box breathing as a fast, physical method for regaining calm in stressful classroom moments, arguing that positive self-talk alone is often too weak to override the body's fight-or-flight response. He explains the technique step by step — inhaling, holding, exhaling, and holding again, each for a count of four — and notes it can take practice to avoid over-inhaling. Linsin frames the core insight as 'change the body's reaction first, and the mind will follow,' positioning box breathing as a way to physically interrupt stress symptoms like a racing heart and tense shoulders. He bolsters the technique's credibility by noting that Navy SEALs use it to maintain composure under extreme conditions. The article closes with a simple, repeatable prompt teachers can use the next time a difficult student or time pressure threatens their composure.
points: Positive self-talk alone is often insufficient to overcome stress because the body's fight-or-flight response is physically powerful and can contradict what the mind is telling itself.
The key insight is to change the body's physical reaction first, and the mind will follow.
Box breathing — inhale for four counts, hold for four, exhale for four, hold for four — is a simple, fast technique to interrupt physical stress symptoms.
It's common to over-inhale at first; the practice should feel gentle and easy, not like gasping for air.
The technique is used by US Navy SEALs to stay calm and perform under pressure, lending it real-world credibility for high-stress classroom moments.
quotes: The problem with this approach, however, is that it’s unpredictable. It doesn’t always work well or very quickly and, too often, thoughts alone aren’t strong enough to overcome the physical symptoms of stress.

The simplest and most effective method I’ve found to do this is called box breathing. The way it works is that as soon as you start feeling stressed, begin counting to four during each of four phases of breathing.
It’s important to note that when you first try box breathing it can take a little while to get the hang of it. It’s common to inhale too deeply and not exhale quite enough.
The US Navy Seals practice box breathing in order to train the body (and mind) not to go into fight-or-flight mode despite ever-present danger swirling around them.
So the next time you’re feeling stressed-out and anxious, the next time difficult students or time constraints start affecting your peace of mind, commence box breathing.
